newsitem.title: USA: Aetna seen unscathed by resignation.
newsitem.headline: Aetna seen unscathed by resignation.

text.p: The surprise resignation of Aetna's president late last week should not present a long-term leadership succession problem for the insurer, analysts said on Monday.
Joseph Sebastianelli, 50, resigned last Friday, citing family reasons.
He was widely considered by analysts as the leading candidate to succeed Ronald Compton as chairman and chief executive of the company.
Compton is scheduled to retire on March 1, 1998.

"Our view is that the management depth is decent enough, and there's not a lot of urgency to the situation, that we (don't) view it with any particular alarm," said Margo Vignola, analyst at Merrill Lynch.
"I think it is business as usual," she said.
"Much as I like Sebastianelli, I don't think that his decision reflects on Aetna's operating performance at all."
At 1525 EDT, Aetna shares were up 2-3/8 to 97-1/8 on volume of 352,000 shares.
Sebastianelli's resignation is effective on June 1.
Aetna spokeswoman Joyce Oberdorf told Reuters that under the terms of Sebastianelli's employment contract, he will receive no severance or special consideration.
She said that by resigning, Sebastianelli gave up some $3.4 million in unvested restricted stock and stock option grants.
Analysts said it was surprising that Sebastianelli was walking away from so much money, but that they saw no evidence of deeper reasons for the resignation.

"The public statement they're making is that he's got personal reasons. I have to believe that if something is that serious on the personal level, that's why you make those kind of decisions," said Robert Hoehn, analyst at Salomon Brothers.
Sebastianelli, a former U.S. Healthcare executive, joined Aetna after its $8 billion acquisition of U.S. Healthcare last July.

"I haven't seen any evidence of what would be another reason, which is that there are problems within the merger," Hoehn said. "For the lack of any other reason, I think we have to take it at face value."

Aetna said that there would be a thorough search for a successor but that they were thinking that the search should be conducted for a new chief executive rather than a president to fill Sebastanelli's position.
"There will be a thorough succession process, considering internal and external candidates," Oberdorf said.
